Baltimore will spend Thursday evening staring at fluorescent posters, and my Jaguars vs Ravens prediction starts in that gallery. MICA's Pinkard Gallery on Mount Royal Avenue opens "Globe Posters for the People" from 5 to 7 p.m., a show about the old print shop whose DayGlo cards sold this town its concerts and fight nights, and my call against the 9.5 is just as loud: Ravens with the points, and the Over 39.5.

The news first, because it's official now. The NFL.com injury report released Wednesday lists Lamar Jackson (thumb) and Tyler Huntley (toe) as Out. Joe Fagnano is the expected starter, per coach Jesse Minter through ESPN, and Fagnano went 10-of-21 with an interception in relief during the loss in Buffalo. Nobody in Baltimore is pretending that's the same offense.

The number agrees with them. DraftKings via ESPN as of Thursday, 7:00 p.m. ET, has Jacksonville −9.5 with an over/under of 39.5. Wednesday evening's consensus was Jacksonville −10. The side came back half a point toward Baltimore, and the total held at 39.5. I still think the number priced Fagnano too hard.

The Formula: Net grades Baltimore Ravens −5.5, Jacksonville Jaguars 0.7 (nflverse play-by-play, Nov 4, 2026).

That's a Jaguars side, but it isn't a 10-point side. Jacksonville is 5-2 and has allowed just 111 points in seven games, and it's 4-1 at home. On the road it's 1-1. Both teams are on 4 days of rest, so nobody gets fresher legs on a short week.

What keeps Baltimore inside the number is Derrick Henry and the ground game. The Ravens run for 4.8 yards a carry. Jacksonville allows 3.4, so it won't be pretty, but a backup quarterback's best friend is a team that keeps handing off and keeps the clock moving. Jacksonville has health questions of its own: Bhayshul Tuten is questionable with an ankle. Baltimore's game-day inactives include corner Nate Wiggins, tackle Emery Jones Jr., defensive tackle Aeneas Peebles, receiver Elijah Sarratt and quarterback Kedon Slovis.

The total is the bigger call. Jacksonville has scored 196 points in seven games, and Baltimore's defense has given up 203 in eight. Short weeks get sloppy, sloppy games hand out short fields, and short fields turn into points. My final is 45, well clear of 39.5.

The room is with me on the side and the Over. The Formula, Next Man Up and Letdown Watch all have Baltimore plus the 9.5 and the Over. Next Man Up is the toughest on the Ravens at Jaguars 26, Ravens 19, and even that lands inside the number. In The Trenches has no pick: Baltimore tackle Emery Jones Jr. is out, and its season numbers were built with him on the field. Follow The Money has no call: the line moved half a point, under the one-point cutoff.

Jacksonville wins the game. Baltimore, with a backup quarterback and a building that still knows how to get loud, loses it by five.

games.fanatic_story:
Owen Pratt was pressed against the glass at MICA's Pinkard Gallery on Mount Royal Avenue a full hour before "Globe Posters for the People" opened on Thursday. The show celebrates the old Baltimore print shop whose fluorescent posters used to scream fight nights and soul revues off every telephone pole in this town, and Owen wanted one with Joe Fagnano's name on it, in letters big enough to read from the upper deck.

Ivy Corcoran, up from Duval in a teal toboggan, read the first poster in the window out loud. "One Night Only." She said that sounded about right for whoever plays quarterback in Baltimore this week.

Owen: Laugh all you want. This town won a Super Bowl with Trent Dilfer.

Ivy: This town won a Super Bowl with a defense that ate people, and a quarterback who handed off and got out of the way.

Owen: Exactly. That's the plan for Thursday. Hand off and get out of the way.

Owen grades every Ravens season with one question: who's hitting people? Ray Lewis and Ed Reed are in Canton, and to Owen they're the measuring stick for every defense this town puts on the field. Lamar Jackson is on injured reserve with a thumb injury from the first snap in Buffalo. Tyler Huntley is on injured reserve with a toe injury from that same afternoon. Owen took that news the way his old man took the Mayflower trucks leaving for Indianapolis: in dead silence, then at full volume for about a week.

Ivy doesn't do feelings. She does standings, folded in her jacket and pulled out like a badge. Jacksonville is 5-2. The Jaguars have given up 111 points in seven games, which she has circled twice in red marker, and they sit on top of the AFC South. Baltimore is 4-4 and 1-2 at home.

Ivy: You want a poster? Print the standings. Big letters. Fluorescent.

Owen: You've been in first place for a month and you act like you invented it.

Ivy: I've been waiting since Tony Boselli was a rookie. I earned the attitude.

Jacksonville fans sat through the years with tarps on the upper-deck seats. Ivy watched every snap of them, so Ravens history doesn't scare her. She just asks what he's done lately.

What Baltimore has lately is Derrick Henry, and Owen will ride that horse until it drops. The Ravens run for 4.8 yards a carry. Ivy fires back that Jacksonville's front gives up only 3.4, and that the Jaguars run for 4.6 against a Baltimore defense that allows 3.8. Thursday turns into a shoving match up front, and neither one wants a track meet.

Owen: Kyle Hamilton is going to play like his hair is on fire. Roquan Smith too. A short week is a street fight, and we're a street-fight town.

Ivy: Your secondary is held together with tape. Wiggins is out. Jones is inactive up front.

Owen: Tuten is questionable on our side. I read the report too.

Ivy gave something up to be here, and she wants credit for it. Back home, JJ Grey & Mofro are playing the Jax Amphitheater on Thursday night at the Greater Jacksonville Agricultural Fair, out at the fair's new home on Normandy Boulevard. She traded swamp rock and a fried-everything food row for a cold parking lot on Russell Street and a Ravens fan who wants to talk about Dilfer.

Owen: You'll catch the fair next week. My quarterback might not catch a break all month.

Ivy: First honest thing you've said since I landed.

Owen's whole game plan fits on a napkin: feed Henry, let Hamilton hit somebody, and let Fagnano throw only when he has to. Ivy folded the napkin into a paper airplane and sailed it into his lap.

Owen buys a poster before kickoff anyway. It says BALTIMORE in screaming orange, and he swears it'll look even better in January.

My call: Jaguars 25, Ravens 20.

A Lombardi Trophy sits inside the Casa de las Alhajas this week, next to a ring from every Super Bowl ever played, and the NFL House in Madrid is where my Bengals vs Falcons prediction starts. Sunday at the Bernabéu, I'm taking Atlanta plus the 3 and the Under 52.5.

The number hasn't moved an inch. The spread and the over/under both opened Cincinnati −3 and 52.5 on Tuesday, and both are still there in the Wednesday evening consensus. Nobody has found a reason to push it, which tells me the market is comfortable calling this a field-goal game. I think it's a little less than that.

The Formula: Net grades Atlanta Falcons −2.2, Cincinnati Bengals −2 (nflverse play-by-play, Nov 4, 2026).

Those two teams grade out almost dead even, and they're meeting in Madrid, not Atlanta. That's the heart of the case. Cincinnati is the better team on paper at 5-2, with 206 points scored and 158 allowed. Atlanta is 3-5 and has been outscored 189 to 171. But even grades and a three-point number leave the Falcons room to lose and still get paid.

The last week explains why the Bengals are laying it. Joe Burrow threw five touchdown passes in an overtime shootout win over Tennessee at home. Atlanta got shut out in Tampa, and Michael Penix Jr. threw four interceptions. That's the freshest picture in everybody's head, and it's exactly the kind of picture that props up a favorite for one more week.

Look at how Atlanta wins instead. Bijan Robinson and the Falcons run for 4.8 yards a carry, and Cincinnati's defense allows 5.0. The Bengals run for only 3.8 against an Atlanta defense that gives up 4.6, so Burrow is carrying the offense with Tee Higgins outside. If Atlanta keeps feeding Robinson, it shortens the game and keeps Burrow on the sideline.

That's also the case for the Under. Both teams have spent a week getting across an ocean, both had to adjust their body clocks, and the first quarter in an international game often looks like it. My final adds up to 48, four and a half points under the number.

The room is split on the side and together on the total. The Formula likes Atlanta and has the Falcons winning outright, Falcons 25, Bengals 24. Next Man Up also takes the points with a two-point Bengals win. Letdown Watch and In The Trenches lay it with Cincinnati, both at four-point margins. All four with a total call are on the Under. Follow The Money has nothing to say, since neither the spread nor the total has budged since the open.

Two of the four cards keep Cincinnati short of the 3, and my final has the Bengals by two. That's where I land.

Manuel Turizo plays the halftime show, the crowd will be half curious and half confused, and Cincinnati escapes Madrid with a win that doesn't quite reach the number.

Bengals 25, Falcons 23. Falcons cover the 3. Under 52.5.

Russ Amundsen walked the whole Dirty Birds Fan Walk on Sunday, from the Paseo de la Castellana all the way to the Bernabéu, flapping his elbows every hundred yards whether anybody asked him to or not. A Spanish grandfather tried it with him for a block, and Russ said it was the best moment of his trip.

Laura Kessel had spent the morning standing in front of the Bengals Menina, the striped statue the team put up for the Madrid art display, and she was still mad nobody had painted it in more stripes.

Laura: You flew five thousand miles to do a chicken dance in the street.

Russ: The Dirty Bird is a sacred tradition. Jamal Anderson invented it so the whole country could watch us have fun.

Laura: The whole country watched you blow the biggest lead in Super Bowl history.

Russ took off his hat, held it against his chest, and said nothing for ten full seconds. Then he put the hat back on and asked whether Cincinnati had ever won a Super Bowl. Laura stopped smiling.

This is the problem with two fan bases that have been hurt this badly. Laura has watched her team lose two Super Bowls to San Francisco and one to the Rams, and she doesn't even blink about the old days anymore. Russ grew up on Michael Vick running around entire defenses, and he still won't talk about the second half of that Super Bowl in New England. Neither one gets to act superior, and both of them try anyway.

Indianapolis is coming off a mess of its own, a five-touchdown loss in Jacksonville. Daniel Jones starts again, and Jonathan Taylor is the reason the Colts can stay in this. Lou Ferraro bought two tickets to Cinderella at Clowes Hall for Friday night, the Indianapolis Ballet's company premiere with the symphony playing live, and he wants everyone to know it wasn't his idea. His wife picked the show. Lou chose the seats, because Lou chooses everything.

Cole Garrison drove up from Dallas on Thursday and immediately asked where the nearest decent barbecue was. Lou handed him a pork tenderloin sandwich the size of a hubcap and told him to stop complaining.

Cole: You're going to the ballet two days before a football game.

Lou: I'm going to watch a girl in rags win when nobody gives her a chance. It's research.

That's the Colts fan's whole mindset this season. Indianapolis is 2-6. Lou has accepted it the way he accepts snow in March, with a lot of grumbling and no plans to leave. But his team just lost by five touchdowns in Jacksonville, and he figures the bottom has already fallen out. There's nowhere left to go but up.

Cole lives on the other end of the emotional scale. Dallas is America's Team, and Cole believes every Cowboys game is a national event. He brings up the five Super Bowl trophies, Roger Staubach, Troy Aikman, Emmitt Smith and Michael Irvin, and he walks like a guy who personally won all of them.

Lou: Five trophies, and the most recent one is older than half the players on your roster.

Cole: At least we have trophies with names people remember.

Lou: Peyton Manning. Reggie Wayne. Marvin Harrison. Dwight Freeney. Want me to keep going?

Cole: No.

Lou has his own Super Bowl memory, the rainy night in Miami with Manning, and he plays it in his head every time a Dallas fan starts bragging. Indianapolis knows how to win the big one. It just hasn't done it in a while.

Cole's real problem is Arizona. Last Sunday the Cowboys had a two-touchdown lead in the fourth quarter and gave the whole thing away. Cole hasn't fully recovered. He keeps saying Dak Prescott didn't lose that game. Lou keeps asking who did.

Cole: CeeDee Lamb is the best receiver on the field Sunday. Write it down.

Lou: Jonathan Taylor is the best player on the field Sunday. I already wrote it down and framed it.

The ground game is where Lou thinks his team takes control. The Colts run for 4.2 yards a carry against a Dallas defense that gives up 5.2. Lou sees Taylor carrying it thirty times and Daniel Jones keeping the chains moving with short throws. Cole says Dallas only runs for 3.8 a carry but doesn't need to, because Prescott throwing to Lamb is the best plan in football.

Lou: Your plan was the best plan in football right up until the fourth quarter last week.

Cole stood up, walked around the block and came back.

Saturday they hit the Indiana State Museum, where the Heroes from the Heartland exhibit closes Sunday. Cole wanted to see it because his grandfather served. Lou took him, bought the tickets and didn't say one word about football for an entire hour. That's how Hoosiers treat a guest. Then they drove past the State Fairgrounds, where the Christmas Nights of Lights opened Friday, and Lou went right back to trash talking.

Lou: You see those lights? That's what our stadium looks like when Taylor breaks a long one.

Cole: That's what your stadium looks like from the parking lot when people leave early.

Cole swears this is the week Dallas finally closes one out. Lou says he's heard that speech every fall since he was ten. Win or lose, Cole is eating another tenderloin sandwich on the way out of town, and he's never going to admit he likes it.

My call: Colts 27, Cowboys 24.

Detroit Lions vs Miami Dolphins in Week 9 shares a Sunday with the NASCAR Cup Series championship at Homestead-Miami Speedway, four hundred miles for the title, green flag at 3 p.m., about two hours after kickoff at Hard Rock Stadium. Martin Sorensen flew down from Detroit for both, because a man from the Motor City doesn't get many chances to watch a championship race and a Lions road win on the same afternoon. Carla Ruiz, who has lived through more Dolphins rebuilds than she can count, asked him to choose one.

Martin: I can do both. Kickoff at one, checkered flag by dinner. That's called planning.

Carla: That's called traffic on the Turnpike. You'll see the last ten laps on your phone.

Martin lives on a clock. He's a window-urgency guy, and the window in Detroit is wide open right now. Jared Goff, Amon-Ra St. Brown, Jahmyr Gibbs, Aidan Hutchinson, a roster built to win now, and Martin wakes up every day afraid that now ends tomorrow. The Lions are 5-2 and have won three straight, the last one an emotional win against Minnesota, and Martin is treating every remaining Sunday like a lap he can't get back.

Martin: You don't waste a car like this one. You don't park it in the garage and admire it. You run it until the tires come off.

Carla: That's a nice speech for a team that's 1-2 on the road.

She's not wrong, and Martin knows it. Detroit is 4-0 at Ford Field and 1-2 everywhere else. The Lions have scored 203 points and allowed 180, which tells you the defense has been bending all fall. The local paper in Michigan called this team injury-riddled this week, and Martin read that headline three times on the plane.

Carla is the opposite kind of fan. She doesn't panic about windows, she studies blueprints. Miami is 1-6 and 0-3 at home, and she'll tell you that's what a teardown looks like from the inside. A first-year head coach in Jeff Hafley, who ran the defense in Green Bay, and a quarterback in Malik Willis who started the last game. Carla isn't asking for a playoff run. She's asking for evidence that the new plan works, and lately she's gotten some.

Carla: Our last four games were all one-score games. You know what a rebuilding team looks like when it's going nowhere? It gets blown out. We aren't getting blown out.

Martin: You're 1-6.

Carla: We're 1-6 and close. There's a difference, and Hafley's defense is the difference.

Miami runs it. Ollie Gordon II has been carrying the load, and the Dolphins get 4.6 yards a carry against a Detroit defense that gives up 4.3. Detroit runs for 4.7 against a Miami defense that allows 4.2, and Gibbs is the kind of back who turns half a yard of daylight into a long afternoon for a defense. That's Martin's whole plan: give it to Gibbs, let Goff work off it, and get out of town.

There's some history pushing Martin along, too. Detroit has won its last two trips to Miami. Carla points out the Dolphins still lead the all-time series, and she says it like a woman who has been waiting all season to win an argument.

Then there's the heat. Early November in South Florida still feels like summer to a guy whose phone is showing Detroit weather. Martin brought one jacket and won't need it.

Carla's ask for Sunday is simple: keep it close, keep Willis upright, and make Detroit earn every yard. Martin's ask is louder. He wants the Lions to put this one away early so he can make it down to Homestead for the finish. Carla told him the Dolphins' rebuild doesn't care about his race schedule.

Somebody wins a championship in Homestead on Sunday evening. Martin just wants the Lions to win something smaller first, on the way to something bigger in January.

My call: Lions 27, Dolphins 22.

Now the concern. Deshaun Watson is in the concussion protocol, and he did not practice Wednesday, along with defensive tackle Maliek Collins and linebacker Quincy Williams. The po-boy lines on Oak Street will be long Sunday, the dome will be half full of nervous Saints fans, and New Orleans scrapes out a win that doesn't reach the number.

Frank Haller showed up at Beignet Fest in City Park on Saturday wearing a brown and orange stocking cap in Louisiana. He had beignet dust on it within ten minutes. He said that was the most Cleveland thing that ever happened to him, and Andre Thibault agreed.

Andre: You came to New Orleans in a winter hat.

Frank: I came to New Orleans in a lucky hat. Different thing.

Andre has lived in the city his whole life and has worn a paper bag to at least one Saints game, which he admits only when pressed. He remembers the years when the team was a joke, and he remembers the night the Superdome reopened after the storm, when Steve Gleason blocked that punt and the whole building shook. That night, he says, is why New Orleans will never quit on this team.

games.fanatic_story:
Ray Donnelly ran the Rocky Steps Challenge at the Philadelphia Museum of Art on Saturday morning, and when he got to the top, he turned around, threw both arms in the air and yelled something about the Giants that can't be printed. A guy from New Jersey a few steps below him yelled something right back.

That guy was Leon Drobny, who came down the Turnpike on Friday to stay with Ray, his old college roommate, for the weekend. They have been fighting about this game since the first week of freshman year.

Leon: You know Rocky lost the first fight, right?

Ray: He went the distance. That's the point. Philly goes the distance.

Leon: Philly is 2-6.

Ray: Philly is a mood, not a record.

Ray is the kind of Eagles fan who takes every insult personally and every loss as a crime against the city. He was there the night the Philly Special won the Super Bowl against New England, and he tells that story every time somebody brings up a bad season, which is lately. He grew up worshipping Reggie White and Brian Dawkins, and he believes any defense that doesn't hit like Dawkins is just a group of guys standing around.

Leon is a Giants fan, which means he carries around a different kind of grudge. Four Super Bowl titles, two of them against the Patriots, one with a guy catching a ball against his helmet. Lawrence Taylor. Michael Strahan. Eli Manning, who Leon still defends like a family member.

Leon: You booed Santa Claus.

Ray: Santa had it coming. Ask anybody who was there.

This week is weird for both of them, because neither quarterback is the guy they expected. Philadelphia benched Tanner McKee on Wednesday and handed Joe Milton his first career start with Jalen Hurts out, and J.J. McCarthy is starting for New York in place of Jameis Winston. Ray calls it the backup bowl. Leon calls it a chance for McCarthy to prove something.

Ray has a bigger worry. Saquon Barkley and DeVonta Smith didn't practice Wednesday, and Ray has been pacing his kitchen ever since. Barkley is the one guy on the team who makes Leon nervous, because Barkley used to be a Giant, and Leon has never forgiven him for leaving.

Leon: If Saquon plays, I'm booing him.

Ray: If Saquon plays, you're going to be booing him from the ground.

The Giants are 4-2-1 and coming off a bye, so they're rested and healthy and Leon is feeling cocky. New York runs for 4.2 yards a carry, and Philadelphia's defense gives up 4.4. Leon thinks the Giants just run it right down the middle all day.

Ray thinks the same about his own team. The Eagles only run for 3.8 a carry, but the Giants give up 5.0, and Ray says that means somebody in green is going to find a crease. He doesn't care who.

Ray: You come into my building with a backup quarterback and expect the crowd to be polite?

Leon: I expect the crowd to be loud for ten minutes and then start booing its own team.

Ray didn't argue that. It's happened before.

Sunday morning, before they head to the stadium, Ray is taking Leon for a cheesesteak in South Philly. Leon has been warned that if he orders it wrong, Ray will leave him on the sidewalk. Leon has been practicing the order in the mirror.

Ray says the Linc is going to shake for a kid making his first start. Leon says he's heard the Linc shake at its own guys plenty. One of them rides home quiet, and Leon is already rehearsing the grin he'll wear up the Turnpike.

My call: Giants 22, Eagles 21.

I've switched sides on this game since Tuesday: Los Angeles minus 4.5 is the call now, with the Under 47.5.

Why the flip? The number came to me. The spread opened Rams −5.5 on Tuesday morning and sits at −4.5 in the consensus as of Wednesday evening, with the over/under steady at 47.5. My final hasn't budged, a five-point Rams win. At five and a half that fell short. At four and a half it clears.

The Formula: Net grades Washington Commanders −5.5, Los Angeles Rams 3.7 (nflverse play-by-play, Nov 4, 2026).

That gap is the biggest piece of this. Los Angeles is 4-4, but it has scored 194 points and allowed 168, the profile of a team better than its record. Washington is 2-4-1 and has been outscored 182 to 159. Matthew Stafford and Sean McVay are 2-1 on the road.

The case for Washington is the building. The Commanders are 2-1-1 at home and 0-3 away, so Northwest Stadium matters. Jayden Daniels gives Dan Quinn an escape hatch on every broken play, and Washington runs for 4.8 yards a carry. But the Rams allow just 4.0, and they run for 5.0 themselves against a Washington defense that also allows 4.0. If Los Angeles stays on schedule on early downs, Stafford gets to choose his spots, and that's when Puka Nacua starts eating.

There's a coaching wrinkle too. Kliff Kingsbury called Washington's offense the last two seasons and now sits on the Rams staff as assistant head coach. He knows what Daniels likes when the pocket closes. That doesn't win a game by itself, but it doesn't hurt.

The trip is real. The Rams fly across the country on a normal week of rest, and Letdown Watch counts that against them, landing at Rams 25, Commanders 21. That's a four-point game, which is exactly why this is close.

My total is 47, half a point shy of the number. That's close, and I won't dress it up. Two offenses that like to run and two defenses that hold up against it should keep the clock moving.

Washington makes it a fight in its own stadium. Los Angeles has the better roster and a coach on its staff who knows the other sideline's playbook by heart, and it pulls away in the fourth.

Claire Benton was on Constitution Avenue at 8 a.m. Sunday for the National Veterans Parade 5K, and by 9 she had her race bib pinned to the dashboard and her car pointed at Landover. She posted her finishing time to the group chat before she hit the Beltway, and nobody asked.

Diane Kerr flew in from Los Angeles on Saturday and stayed on Claire's couch, which Claire now regrets.

Diane: You ran three miles before a football game.

Claire: I ran three miles so I could scream for four hours without guilt. That's called structure.

Structure is Claire's whole religion. She was raised on Joe Gibbs, three Super Bowl titles with three different quarterbacks, and she figures that's the only proof anybody needs. Build the machine, plug in the guy, win. She talks about the Hogs up front like they're family, and she'll bring up Sammy Baugh before you finish saying hello. To Claire, the building wins first and the big names show up second.

Diane has a different religion. She follows coaching trees, and she can draw the Sean McVay branch on the back of a parking stub from memory. Then she tells you where every assistant ended up and whether he was any good. This week she gets to rub one branch right in Claire's face.

Diane: Kliff Kingsbury. Called your offense two straight years. Now he's ours.

Claire: You can have him.

Diane: We did take him. That's the point. He knows every call Daniels likes when the pocket closes.

Claire didn't answer that one. She just stared out the window at the parade crowd breaking up near the Archives.

Washington is 2-4-1, and Claire won't pretend it's a good team. But the Commanders are 2-1-1 at home and haven't won on the road all year, and she figures this is a Northwest Stadium game, not a road game, so it counts. Jayden Daniels can turn a busted play into a first down with his legs, and Washington runs for 4.8 yards a carry. Claire likes that.

Diane likes her own ground game more. The Rams run for 5.0 a carry and give up 4.0, and Matthew Stafford has been doing this so long that he's seen every blitz Dan Quinn has ever drawn up. She brings up Puka Nacua the way some people bring up their kids.

Diane: Stafford on early downs with a clean pocket is a surgeon. You know what Nacua does after the catch.

Claire: I know what our crowd does when a surgeon has to work fast.

The Rams have history too, and Diane is happy to recite it. The Fearsome Foursome, Deacon Jones and Merlin Olsen chasing quarterbacks into the bleachers. The Greatest Show on Turf, Kurt Warner and Marshall Faulk running up scores in a dome. Two Super Bowl titles, XXXIV and LVI.

Claire: Your team has lived in three cities. Ours has lived in one zip code and suffered in it honestly.

Diane: Suffered honestly. Put that on a shirt.

Claire's real fear isn't Stafford or Nacua. It's the trip. She thinks the Rams fly across the country, start slow, and Washington gets a couple of early stops with the crowd going nuts. Diane's fear is simpler. Daniels gets loose once and turns one broken play into seven points, and the whole stadium decides it's the old days again.

Diane: Antonio Williams worries me more than you'd think.

Claire: Good. He should.

They stopped for gas off Route 50 and argued about whether Kingsbury would get booed. Claire said yes, loudly and for the entire first quarter. Diane said nobody in the upper deck would know which one he was. Claire said they'd know. They always know.

Claire has her bib in the window and her voice saved for Kingsbury. Diane has a Stafford jersey and no shame about wearing it in Landover. They'll share the parking spot, share the ride home, and not say one word to each other in the fourth quarter.

My call: Rams 26, Commanders 21.

games.fanatic_story:
Ruth Calder flew in from Denver on Friday, and the first thing Mitch Kovac did was drive her out to the Carolina Renaissance Festival. He told her it was a cultural experience. She spent two hours watching grown men joust on horseback, ate a turkey leg the size of her forearm and declared it the best thing about the whole state.

Mitch: That's not the best thing about the state.

Ruth: It's the best thing about this weekend so far.

Mitch has been a Panthers fan since the team was born, and he takes everything about the franchise personally. He remembers Sam Mills and the Keep Pounding speech. He remembers Jake Delhomme and the Super Bowl in Houston, and he remembers Cam Newton dabbing his way through a season where Carolina looked unbeatable.

Then he remembers the Super Bowl in Santa Clara, and Ruth is the person who reminds him.

Ruth: Von Miller. Strip sack. You remember that, right?

Mitch: I remember everything about that night. I just don't talk about it.

Ruth is a Broncos fan who grew up on John Elway, and she has the attitude to match. Three Super Bowl titles. The helicopter run. Two straight rings at the end of Elway's career, then Peyton Manning riding off with one more. She brings up the orange crush defense like she's talking about a family heirloom.

Denver is 6-2, and Ruth has been insufferable about it. But she knows the Broncos have been a different team away from Mile High. They're 4-0 at home and 2-2 on the road, and Mitch keeps reminding her of that every time she starts bragging.

Mitch: Your team plays great when the other guys can't breathe. Down here we have air.

Ruth: Down here you have humidity. It's like playing inside a gym bag.

Carolina is 3-4, and Mitch is fine with that, because he thinks the Panthers are about to turn it around. Bryce Young has been getting better, and Tetairoa McMillan is the receiver Mitch has wanted for years. The Panthers played last Thursday, so they've had ten days to rest up while Denver comes in on a normal week. Mitch sees that as a big deal.

Ruth sees Bo Nix as the bigger deal. She thinks Nix is the best young quarterback in the conference and that Jaylen Waddle gives Denver a weapon Carolina can't handle. Mitch says Waddle is fast, but the Panthers have speed too.

The ground game is where both of them get loud. Denver runs for 4.0 yards a carry and Carolina allows 4.6. Carolina runs for 4.3 and Denver also allows 4.6. Mitch thinks both teams are going to be pounding it inside all afternoon. Ruth says that's fine, because her guys are tougher.

Saturday afternoon they walked through the Carolinas Veterans Day Festival at Romare Bearden Park. Ruth's dad served in the Air Force, and Mitch's grandfather was in the Army. Both of them got quiet for a while, and neither one said a word about football. Then they walked past the Spectrum Center, where the Ally Tipoff is bringing college hoops to town on Sunday, and Ruth asked if Charlotte only cared about basketball.

Mitch: This is a football town.

Ruth: This is a basketball town that happens to have a football team.

Mitch got so loud on the sidewalk that a family crossed the street.

Ruth flies home Monday with a turkey leg story and, she says, a win. Mitch says the turkey leg is the only thing she's taking out of Charlotte. He's already planning the Ren Fest rematch, jousting seats included.

My call: Broncos 24, Panthers 22.

He's 0-7 this season and he still bought new seats. Nate Coleman, in town from Houston, can't decide whether that's loyal or crazy.

Nate: You know you could just stay home, right?

Marty: Staying home is how you lose a team. Ask San Diego.

That one hurts Marty more than it hurts anybody. The Chargers left San Diego, and plenty of fans down there never forgave them. Marty kept the faith, and now he sits in an Inglewood stadium full of visiting fans who outnumber him most Sundays. He brings up Dan Fouts and Air Coryell, LaDainian Tomlinson and Junior Seau, and he does it like a man trying to remind himself why he still cares.

Nate understands the pain. Houston lost the Oilers to Tennessee, and the city had to wait years for a new team. When the Texans finally showed up, Nate was there for the first game. He remembers Andre Johnson catching everything thrown his way, and J.J. Watt wrecking offensive game plans every Sunday. He also remembers that the Texans have never made it to a conference title game.

Nate: At least we've been to the playoffs lately.

Marty: At least we've been to a Super Bowl.

Nate: You got blown out in it.

Marty: We were there. You've never been there.

Nate dropped the subject.

The Chargers are 0-7 and have scored only 99 points all year. Marty doesn't dress it up. Justin Herbert gets hit too much, nothing seems to go right in the fourth quarter, and the team has found every way possible to lose. But Marty still thinks Herbert can carry them, and he loves Omarion Hampton. He thinks Hampton is the kind of back who could change the whole mood of the season with one big afternoon.

Houston is 2-5, and the Texans haven't won at home all season. They are coming off a bye, though, and Nate thinks two weeks of rest gives C.J. Stroud time to reset. He has seen enough of Stroud's good days to keep showing up.

Marty's worry is his own defense. Khalil Mack, Deane Leonard and Kendall Williamson all missed practice Wednesday, and Derwin James is already on injured reserve. Marty kept checking his phone during lunch and finally just turned it off.

Nate: That's half your defense sitting out.

Marty: Mack has played through worse. I'm not panicking until Saturday.

games.fanatic_story:
Glen Tolliver got to Patriot Place Plaza on Saturday early enough to stake out a spot right up front for Rob Gronkowski's Patriots Hall of Fame induction. He wore the old number 87 jersey, the one with the grass stain he refuses to wash out, and he spiked an imaginary football every time the crowd chanted Gronk's name.

Paul Lindgren, up from Green Bay for the weekend, stood next to him in a Packers parka and politely clapped for a tight end who used to run through his team's secondary like it owed him rent.

Glen: Nine seasons. Three rings with us. The most fun player this franchise ever had.

Paul: He was fun. I'll give you fun. Now ask me how many championships Green Bay has.

Glen: Please don't.

Paul: Thirteen.

Paul counts titles the way some guys count push-ups, out loud and with his chest out. He goes back to Curly Lambeau, then Vince Lombardi and Bart Starr on the frozen field, then Brett Favre and Aaron Rodgers. To Paul, the Packers aren't a franchise. They're a town that happens to own a football team, and every fan in it acts like a part owner because a lot of them are.

Glen has his own numbers, and they're more recent. Six Super Bowl titles in New England, all of them in the lifetime of anybody younger than forty. He was in the stands for the snow games, the comebacks and the parades through Boston. He doesn't care about leather helmets. He cares about what happened on his watch.

Glen: You've got history. We've got the receipts that still have ink on them.

Paul: Your receipts all have the same two names on them.

That's the shot every Patriots fan hears eventually, and Glen has an answer ready. This team is 5-3 and 3-0 at home with Drake Maye throwing it and Mike Vrabel on the sideline. Different names, same building, same attitude.

The Packers are 5-3 too, and Paul likes how fresh they are. Green Bay played last Thursday, so the Packers walk into Foxborough with ten full days of rest. Jordan Love has had time to heal up and get his reads right, and Paul thinks that matters more than anything said at a podium this week.

Glen's worry list is longer. A.J. Brown, TreVeyon Henderson, Hunter Henry and Christian Barmore all sat out Wednesday's practice, and Glen has refreshed the team site so often his thumb hurts. He keeps telling himself it's one practice.

Paul: Your best receiver, your back, your tight end and your big guy up front. That's not a practice report. That's a cry for help.

Glen: It's Wednesday. Ask me on Sunday.

Neither one expects a shootout. Green Bay runs for 3.1 yards a carry, and the Patriots aren't much better at 4.4, with both defenses giving up 4.0. Glen sees a slugfest decided by whoever wins the turnover battle. Paul sees Love hitting one deep shot to change everything.

After the induction, they wandered past the Bass Pro Shops to see Santa's arrival at 5 o'clock, because Glen's nephew made him promise. Paul stood in a crowd of kids and told every one of them that Santa is a Packers fan. Glen told every one of them that Santa lives in the North Pole, which is basically New England.

Paul: He comes down chimneys in Wisconsin first. Everybody knows that.

Glen: He'd freeze to death in Green Bay before he got to the second house.

Glen is still riding the Gronk weekend and says nothing can bring him down. Paul says that's fine. He'll be the guy in the parka in the third quarter, clapping politely again, only this time for his own team.

My call: Patriots 24, Packers 21.

Vic grew up in Oakland. His dad took him to the Coliseum for games when he was a kid, and he still talks about the old Black Hole like it was church. When the Raiders left for Las Vegas, Vic didn't follow them. He stayed in the Bay and kept his season tickets in his heart, if not in his wallet.

Nora: You still root for a team that left you.

Vic: I root for the shield. The city doesn't matter.

Nora shakes her head every time he says that. She grew up watching Joe Montana and Jerry Rice, then Steve Young, and she can name every 49ers Super Bowl team without stopping to think. Five titles. She brings that up every time Vic gets loud.

Vic reminds her the Raiders have three, and that his team was winning titles while she was still learning to walk.

The 49ers are 6-1 and unbeaten at home. They're coming off a bye, and Nora spent the week off with nothing to do but read injury news. That turned out to be a bad idea. Christian McCaffrey, Trent Williams, Mike Evans and Deebo Samuel Sr. all missed Wednesday's practice.

Nora: Four guys. Four.

Vic: Sounds like you're in trouble.

Nora: Sounds like you've never seen Brock Purdy handle a mess.

She has a point. Purdy has spent his career being doubted and then proving people wrong. Nora loves that about him. She also loves George Kittle, because Kittle plays like every snap is the last one he'll ever get. If Kittle is healthy, Nora isn't worried.

Vic says Bowers could be the best tight end in football in a couple of years, and Nora, a Kittle fan, gets very quiet whenever he says it.

Vic: You know I'm right.

Nora: I know Kittle's still here.

The Raiders' problem is the running game. They've barely been able to run it all year. Vic knows it. He says Cousins will have to throw forty times, and he says it like he's already tired.

Kara Holm's garage in Ballard still has the confetti. She swept up a handful of the blue and green stuff after the Super Bowl parade last February and put it in a jar on the shelf next to her toolbox. Every time a friend stops by, she shows it to them. Neil Carver, her cousin from Phoenix, has seen the jar six times this week.

Neil: I get it. You won.

Kara: We won by sixteen. Against the Patriots. I want you to really get it.

The Seahawks beat New England twenty-nine to thirteen in Super Bowl sixty, and Kara still talks about it like it happened last weekend. She remembers where she was sitting, what she was eating, and how long she yelled when the clock hit zero. She also remembers the long years before it, when the only title her team had was from the Russell Wilson days, and people around the league kept saying Seattle had peaked.

Neil doesn't have a jar. The Cardinals have been around longer than almost any team in the NFL, and the closest they've come to a Super Bowl title was that heartbreaker against Pittsburgh. Neil was a kid then. He still remembers Larry Fitzgerald running down the sideline, and he still remembers the final drive that took it all away.

Kara: At least you had Fitz.

Neil: Fitz was the best receiver of his era.

Kara: And he never got a ring.

Neil didn't say anything for a while after that.

This year, Seattle is 4-4. The Seahawks just lost to the Bears on Monday night, and Kara watched the whole thing with her arms crossed. Then Wednesday got worse. Sam Darnold hurt his quad on the last drive, and he's out for Sunday. The backup is coming off a sore elbow, and Kara says she's fine with it because he already beat Arizona thirty-one to seven back in Week 2. She says it a little too fast. She thinks Jaxon Smith-Njigba is one of the best receivers in the league, and she'll argue with anyone who says otherwise.

Neil's Cardinals are 3-5, but they've played well on the road, and they have a new guy at quarterback too. Arizona handed the job to Gardner Minshew this week. Neil says Minshew plays like a guy who's been told no his whole career and never listened. Kara says all she remembers is the mustache. Neil says she'll remember the throws.

He also loves Trey McBride. McBride catches everything, and he plays tight end like a wide receiver with a linebacker's attitude. Neil thinks McBride could have a huge day if Seattle focuses too much on stopping the run.

The two of them spent Saturday at the Seattle Sauna Festival at the National Nordic Museum. Neil had never been to a sauna festival. He said Phoenix is basically a sauna from May to October and he didn't understand why anyone would pay for one. Then he spent forty-five minutes inside and came out saying it was the best thing he'd done all year.

Kara made him jump into the cold tub afterward. Neil yelled loud enough to scare a family out of the next room.

Later, they watched the Sounders host LAFC. Neil wanted to cheer for LA just to needle Kara, but he couldn't bring himself to cheer for anything from California.

Sunday, they're heading to Lumen Field. Kara has her lucky Super Bowl shirt, the one that hasn't been washed since February. Neil has his red Fitzgerald jersey and a stocking cap he borrowed from Kara because he didn't pack for November in Seattle.

Kara: You're wearing my hat to root against my team.

Neil: Your hat. My team.

Kara's hat goes back on her head Sunday night either way. Neil just wants to hand it back with a Cardinals win stuffed inside. The only thing they've settled is that neither of them is ever getting back in that cold tub.

My call: Seahawks 24, Cardinals 19.

Ringling Bros. wraps up its weekend run at Allstate Arena in Rosemont on Sunday, and the Chicago History Museum closes its "Aquí en Chicago" exhibit the same afternoon. My Buccaneers vs Bears pick is Tampa Bay plus the 6.5, and the Under 47.5, after the circus leaves town.

The market has nudged a little toward Chicago. The Bears opened at −6 on Tuesday and sit at −6.5 in the Wednesday evening consensus. The over/under went from 46.5 to 47.5. Neither move is big enough to change my read, and the half point helps the Tampa Bay side.

The Formula: Net grades Chicago Bears −3.7, Tampa Bay Buccaneers −4.5 (nflverse play-by-play, Nov 4, 2026).

That's less than a point between them, and 6.5 is a long way from that.

Chicago is 6-2 and 3-1 at home, with 214 points scored and 160 allowed. The Bears beat Seattle 34-17 on Monday night, so they get only six days before this one. Tampa Bay is 3-5 but 2-1 on the road, with 178 scored and 151 allowed. The Bucs' defense has kept them in a lot of games.

The run game favors Tampa Bay. The Bucs run for 5.1 yards a carry, and the Chicago defense gives up 4.3. Bucky Irving can carry the offense when Baker Mayfield needs help. Chicago runs for 4.3, and Tampa Bay allows only 3.8.

Caleb Williams has been playing well, and Luther Burden III gives him another target. But a short week after a big Monday win is a classic spot for a flat first half. I see Chicago winning, but by four, not by a touchdown.

The Under fits that kind of game. Tampa Bay wants to run the ball and keep Williams on the sideline. Chicago is coming off a short week. My final is 44, three and a half under the number.

Most of the room is on Tampa Bay. The Formula has it Bears 23, Bucs 21. Next Man Up is 25-22, and In The Trenches is 23-19, all three on the Bucs plus the points. Letdown Watch is the only card laying the 6.5, with a 26-19 final.

The total is lopsided in the room. The Formula, Next Man Up, Letdown Watch and In The Trenches are all on the Under. Follow The Money is the lone Over after the one-point rise.

Rosemont gets the circus. Soldier Field gets a Bears team on short rest, and Tampa Bay gets close enough to cover.

games.fanatic_story:
Walt Brenner took his grandkids to the circus on Friday night. Ringling Bros. is at Allstate Arena all weekend, and Walt figured it was a good way to spend an evening before the biggest Bears game of the season so far. The kids loved the acrobats. Walt spent the whole time talking about Caleb Williams.

Sal Ferris, his old Army buddy from Tampa, flew in Saturday morning to see the game. When Walt told him about the circus, Sal said that was a perfect warmup for watching the Bears play football.

Walt: You want to say that again in front of my wife?

Sal: I'd rather say it in front of the scoreboard.

Walt and Sal have been arguing about football since they met at basic training. Walt is Chicago through and through. He was a teenager when the Monsters of the Midway won the Super Bowl, and he can still do the whole Super Bowl Shuffle if you give him enough room. He'll tell you about Walter Payton and Mike Singletary and Dick Butkus, and he'll tell you that Chicago football is about defense, period.

Sal grew up on the creamsicle Bucs, the orange uniforms and the losing seasons. He stuck with them through the bad years and got rewarded twice. First came the Super Bowl with Jon Gruden and that defense. Then came Tom Brady and the second ring. Sal says he's earned the right to talk.

Sal: Two rings. How many you got?

Walt: One. But ours came with a song.

This year the Bears are 6-2, and Walt is having the time of his life. They just beat Seattle on Monday night, and Walt says Caleb Williams finally looks like the guy Chicago has been waiting for since the Sid Luckman days. Walt says Luther Burden III has hands like glue, and he can't stop talking about the way Burden goes up for the ball.

Sal's Bucs are 3-5, and he knows they need a win. But he says Baker Mayfield is the toughest quarterback in the league, and Bucky Irving can run through anybody. Sal saw Irving break a tackle earlier this season that he says he still dreams about.

Walt: You dream about running backs?

Sal: I dream about winning in Chicago.

On Sunday afternoon, before the game, they're going to the Chicago History Museum for the closing of "Aquí en Chicago." Walt's wife says it's the best exhibit she's seen in years, and Walt is going because she told him he was going. Sal is going because he thinks it'll be warmer inside than anywhere else in the city.

Then they'll head to Soldier Field. Walt has his old orange and navy Payton jersey and the same knit hat he's worn to every big game for twenty years. Sal has his Mayfield jersey and three layers of thermal shirts underneath, because he hasn't been north in November since basic training and he remembers how it felt.

Walt: You're going to freeze.

Sal: I've been frozen before. I'm from Tampa, not the moon.

Walt has waited his whole life to feel this good about a Bears quarterback, and he's not letting a guy from Tampa ruin it. Sal says he didn't come to ruin it. He came to watch Irving run through it.

Walt's grandkids have already picked their side. They want the Bears, the acrobats and another night at the circus, in that order. Sal says he'll settle for the circus.

My call: Bears 24, Buccaneers 20.

This is two 6-1 teams, both on eight days' rest, and the market hasn't moved on the side. Buffalo opened at −3.5 and is still −3.5 in the Wednesday evening consensus. The over/under slipped from 46 to 45.5.

The Formula: Net grades Minnesota Vikings −6.3, Buffalo Bills 3.7 (nflverse play-by-play, Nov 4, 2026).

This one is strange. Buffalo grades out as the much better team, and the Formula likes the Bills to cover. But Minnesota is 6-1 while grading out below zero, which tells you the Vikings have won close games and relied on defense. They've allowed only 93 points all season, the fewest in this matchup by a long way.

Buffalo is 6-1 and 3-0 on the road, with 233 points scored and 181 allowed. The Bills beat Baltimore 36-10 last time out. Minnesota is 6-1 and 3-0 at home, with 140 scored and 93 allowed. The Vikings' only loss was 19-15 at Detroit.

Josh Allen and James Cook III give Buffalo the better offense. The Bills run for 5.1 yards a carry, and Minnesota allows 4.6. Kyler Murray and Aaron Jones Sr. run for 4.3 against a Buffalo defense that allows 4.0. Murray came out of the Detroit game with a sore hamstring, and Kevin O'Connell says he starts if he's healthy. That's one more reason to expect a low game.

I think Buffalo wins. But a Minnesota team that's unbeaten at home and plays defense like this is hard to beat by four. A field goal game is the most likely result, and that's inside the number.

The Under fits the Vikings. Minnesota has scored only 140 points in seven games, and their games have stayed low. My final is 45, half a point under.

The cards are split three to one on the side. The Formula is the only card laying the 3.5, with a Bills 27, Vikings 19 final. Next Man Up has Bills 23, Vikings 22. In The Trenches is close too, Bills 22, Vikings 20. Letdown Watch goes all the way to a Minnesota win, Vikings 25, Bills 24.

The total is split too. Next Man Up and In The Trenches are on the Under. The Formula and Letdown Watch are on the Over. Follow The Money sits it out with nothing moving.

The Gophers take care of Saturday at Huntington Bank Stadium, and the Dakota takes care of Monday night's music before the game. Minnesota takes care of the cover.

games.fanatic_story:
Erik Dahl painted his face purple for the first time since college on Saturday. It wasn't even for the Vikings. He was at Huntington Bank Stadium watching the Gophers play UCLA on Salute to Service day, and he got carried away. By the second quarter he was leading his whole row in the ROW chant. By halftime his face paint was running down his neck.

Ellen Marsh, his sister-in-law from Buffalo, was sitting next to him. She had flown in early for the Monday game, and she spent the whole afternoon trying to pretend she didn't know him.

Ellen: You're a grown man.

Erik: I'm a grown man with a team that's 6-1.

Ellen: So am I. And mine actually scores.

That's been the fight all week. Erik's Vikings are 6-1 and unbeaten at home. Their only loss was a close one in Detroit, and Erik still hasn't forgiven the refs. He loves this defense. He says it's the best Vikings defense he's seen since the Purple People Eaters, and he says it like he was there for the Purple People Eaters, which he wasn't.

Ellen's Bills are 6-1 too, and they just crushed Baltimore. Ellen thinks Josh Allen is the best quarterback in football, and she won't hear any argument. She's been a Bills fan her whole life, through four straight Super Bowl losses in the early nineties, the long playoff drought after that, and all the years of coming close with Allen.

Erik: Four Super Bowls. Four losses.

Ellen: Four Super Bowls. How many trips has your team made since the seventies?

Erik had to think about it. Then he stopped thinking about it and changed the subject.

The truth is, both fan bases know heartbreak. The Vikings have been to four Super Bowls and lost them all too. Erik knows it. He just doesn't like hearing it from Ellen.

Erik's big hope is Kyler Murray, sore hamstring and all. Murray came to Minnesota and has been everything Erik wanted. He runs, he throws on the run, and he makes the kind of plays that get a dome on its feet. Erik loves Aaron Jones Sr. almost as much. He says Jones runs like a guy who's angry at the ground.

Ellen counters with James Cook III. Cook can turn any carry into a touchdown, and Ellen says he's the best running back the Bills have had since Thurman Thomas. Erik says Ellen says that about every Bills running back.

On Monday afternoon, before the game, they're going to the Dakota to catch the Blind Boys of Alabama. Ellen's husband bought the tickets months ago. Erik thinks it's a strange way to warm up for a football game. Ellen thinks it's the only way to keep Erik from painting his face again.

Then they'll walk to U.S. Bank Stadium. Erik has his Randy Moss jersey, the one he's had since high school. Ellen has her Allen jersey and a Bills knit hat with the pom-pom on top. She's planning to wear the hat indoors, just to make a point.

Erik: It's a dome. You don't need a hat.

Ellen: I'm from Buffalo. I always need a hat.

Erik wants the dome so loud that Allen can't hear himself think. Ellen says Allen doesn't need to think, he just needs the ball. Erik says that's the dumbest thing he's heard all week, then admits it might be true.

Thanksgiving is three weeks out, and they'll both be at the same table. One of them is going to spend the whole meal hearing about Monday night.

My call: Bills 24, Vikings 21.
